strengths: CHEEM makes a useful contribution to task-incremental visual learning by combining dynamic projection-layer reuse/adaptation with task-similarity-guided architecture sampling. The method is technically coherent, and preserving previously used parameters and task-specific paths provides a sound mechanism for avoiding forgetting under the stated task-ID assumption.

The main empirical gains are substantial: on VDD, CHEEM achieves 83.44 ± 0.50% versus 80.08 ± 0.10% for the modified L2P baseline and 78.14 ± 0.54% for L2G with β-DARTS (Table 2). Results on the 5-Dataset benchmark and under independent task-to-task transfer provide additional support.

The strongest evidence concerns the proposed HEE sampler. It improves over uniform sampling from 76.45% to 83.44% (Table 4); Figure 7 shows that simply extending uniform-sampling training does not close the gap. Four additional task orders, each evaluated over three seeds, support the robustness of this finding (Table 13).

The supplementary ablations substantiate meaningful design tradeoffs. Projection-based CHEEM outperforms Query/Key/Value variants, while FFN-based CHEEM achieves higher accuracy at more than twice the added parameter cost (Table 11). Table 12 also transparently reports the accuracy-versus-complexity tradeoff induced by adapter shortcuts.

The manuscript provides substantial implementation detail, including dataset splits, augmentation, optimization, evolutionary search settings, and baseline modifications. Overall, the demonstrated sampling improvement and accuracy–parameter tradeoff favor acceptance despite the attribution and efficiency reservations below.
weaknesses: The experiments do not isolate whether HEE benefits specifically from meaningful task similarity. Relative to uniform sampling, HEE changes both the sampling hierarchy and the operation probabilities. Controls using constant or shuffled similarities, or a fixed reuse-biased distribution, are absent. Thus, the large HEE-versus-PE gain establishes the effectiveness of the complete sampler, but does not establish the claimed causal role of learned task synergies.

The benefit of architecture search over simpler task-specific adaptation remains insufficiently quantified. There is no matched-budget baseline that installs fixed projection adapters at every layer without search. Independent task-to-task CHEEM also achieves higher accuracy than sequential CHEEM (84.65% versus 83.44%), albeit with greater parameter growth. The evidence therefore supports a compactness benefit more clearly than a positive accuracy benefit from cross-task reuse. Given the acknowledged inheritance from L2G and SPOS, these distinctions matter for assessing originality.

Efficiency reporting is incomplete. The quoted 0.17G versus 2.02G FLOPs compares additional inference computation, not total model cost. Training also requires evaluating previous task networks on new-task data, supernet optimization, evolutionary search, and retraining, but wall-clock time and peak memory are not reported. Furthermore, negative parameter increments in architecture figures reflect smaller active task paths; they cannot represent reductions in persistent storage when old paths must remain available. These quantities should be distinguished.

Some central implementation choices are underexplained in the manuscript, including the adapter bottleneck width and exact CLS extraction point. Adding adapter shortcuts only after architecture selection also changes the function being searched versus the one ultimately trained; Table 12 measures its practical tradeoff but does not explain the reliability of architecture ranking under this mismatch. These are reproducibility and interpretation concerns rather than evidence that the reported results are invalid.

strengths: CHEEM provides a useful approach to exemplar-free task-incremental learning: it selectively reuses, adapts, adds, or skips attention components while preserving previous task pathways. The principal contribution is the task-similarity-guided hierarchical search, building on existing dynamic expansion and single-path NAS methods.

The reported improvements are substantial within the evaluated setting. On VDD, CHEEM achieves 83.44 ± 0.50% versus 80.08 ± 0.10% for adapted L2P and 78.14 ± 0.54% for L2G with β-DARTS (Table 2). It also achieves the highest reported mean on the 5-Dataset benchmark, 94.82% (Table 6). Comparisons among these methods use the same pretrained ViT backbone.

The ablation evidence is stronger than a single benchmark comparison. HEE improves over uniform exploration from 76.45% to 83.44% (Table 4), remains better when uniform exploration receives substantially more training (Figure 7), and performs consistently better across four additional task orders (Table 13). Table 11 supports the projection layer as a reasonable accuracy–parameter tradeoff, while transparently showing that FFN adaptation achieves higher accuracy.

The appendix supplies dataset splits, augmentation policies, optimization settings, evolutionary-search parameters, and baseline modifications. Overall, the demonstrated practical gains and substantial ablations favor weak acceptance, despite unresolved attribution and efficiency concerns.
weaknesses: The experiments do not isolate the value of task similarity from the other changes introduced by HEE. Relative to uniform exploration, HEE changes both the sampling hierarchy and operation probabilities, affecting the preference for reuse and adaptation. A hierarchical sampler with constant or shuffled similarity scores is missing. Consequently, the large gains establish the effectiveness of the combined sampler but do not establish that meaningful task-synergy estimation is the decisive mechanism.

The incremental benefit of transferring knowledge between successive tasks remains unclear. CHEEM's independent task-to-task variant achieves 84.65%, compared with 83.44% for sequential learning (Tables 5 and 2), although it introduces more parameters. This suggests a useful compactness tradeoff, but there is no matched-capacity comparison against independently trained task-specific adapters or projections. Zero forgetting follows from preserving old pathways; it does not independently validate the task-synergy mechanism.

Efficiency claims need more careful accounting. Section 3.1.1 compares added FLOPs of 0.17G and 2.02G, which does not establish a tenfold difference in total inference cost. Figure 4 labels negative parameter differences as new task-specific parameters, although skipping a component cannot remove weights still required by older tasks. Total retained storage, active-path parameters, peak memory, and training/search costs should be distinguished. In particular, inference through all previous task networks, supernet training, evolutionary search, and retraining are not captured by the reported inference overhead.

Baseline coverage limits the broad claims of superiority. Appendix F changes L2P to task-ID-based prompt retrieval and states that it then differs from S-Prompts only in initialization, making these comparisons less independent than their names suggest. The supplied comparisons remain informative for the stated task-incremental setting, but they do not establish superiority over the broader range of pretrained-transformer continual-learning methods.

Some implementation choices remain insufficiently specified in the manuscript, including the adaptation MLP's bottleneck width and activation. Architecture selection also evaluates adaptation without a shortcut, whereas final training adds one; Table 12 measures the resulting tradeoff but does not establish how faithfully search-time rankings predict final performance. These are reproducibility and methodological limitations rather than evidence that the reported results are invalid.

strengths: CHEEM provides a useful contribution to task-incremental visual learning: dynamically selecting reuse, adaptation, new projections, or attention skipping within a pretrained ViT. Although it builds on learning-to-grow and SPOS, the task-similarity-guided hierarchical sampler is a meaningful methodological addition.

The main results support its effectiveness. On VDD, CHEEM achieves 83.44 ± 0.50% versus 80.08 ± 0.10% for the adapted L2P baseline (Table 2). On 5-Dataset, it achieves 94.82 ± 0.02%, the highest reported mean among the compared methods (Table 6). Comparisons generally share the same pretrained backbone.

The sampling ablations are substantial: HEE improves over uniform exploration from 76.45% to 83.44% (Table 4), remains better when uniform exploration receives substantially more training (Figure 7), and consistently outperforms it across four additional task orders (Table 13). This supports the practical value of the proposed search strategy.

The projection-layer choice has direct empirical support beyond the preliminary transfer study. Table 11 shows better accuracy and lower parameter growth than using query, key, or value components; using FFNs improves accuracy but more than doubles parameter growth. This establishes a useful accuracy–capacity tradeoff.

The manuscript specifies data splits, optimization settings, search hyperparameters, baseline adaptations, and multiple-seed evaluations. Preserving previous task paths and weights provides a technically sound mechanism for avoiding forgetting under the explicitly stated task-ID assumption. Overall, these supported contributions favor weak acceptance.
weaknesses: The experiments do not fully isolate why HEE works. Compared with uniform operation sampling, HEE changes both the hierarchical allocation of probability and its dependence on CLS similarity. A hierarchy with constant or shuffled similarities would distinguish useful task-related information from a generic preference for reuse and adaptation. The architectural visualizations alone do not establish that the measured similarities predict transfer.

The necessity of architecture search relative to simpler parameter-efficient alternatives remains insufficiently established. There is no matched-capacity fixed projection-adapter baseline in the sequential setting. Moreover, task-to-task CHEEM reaches 84.65%, versus 83.44% for sequential CHEEM, albeit with greater parameter growth. The demonstrated benefit of cross-task reuse is therefore primarily compactness rather than improved predictive transfer.

Efficiency claims need narrower interpretation. The quoted approximately tenfold advantage over L2P concerns additional FLOPs, not total inference cost. End-to-end training time and peak memory are not reported despite supernet training, evolutionary search, retraining, and evaluating previous task networks to obtain similarities. Negative parameter increments in architecture figures describe active task paths; skipped weights still need storage for earlier tasks.

The comparison set limits the breadth of the superiority claim. L2P and S-Prompts are modified for task-ID routing, and several other methods are adapted from CNNs. These are useful comparisons, but they do not establish superiority over contemporary ViT continual-learning methods generally. Evaluation also uses only one backbone configuration and short task sequences, leaving long-stream expert growth and adaptation depth untested.

Some reproducibility and presentation details remain incomplete: the adaptation MLP's hidden width and activation are not specified in the manuscript, and uniform sampling is described inconsistently between Section 2.2.4 and Figure 6 regarding adaptation candidates. The introduction also overstates restrictions of class-incremental learning, such as equal class counts per task. These are correctable issues rather than fundamental defects.

strengths: CHEEM provides a useful architecture-adaptive approach to exemplar-free continual learning, combining reuse, LoRA adaptation, new modules, and block skipping with task-similarity-guided search. Its contribution is primarily this integration and sampling strategy; the paper appropriately credits prior work for task-centroid routing and learning-to-grow.

The matched LoRA-CL comparison supports the value of architecture search beyond changing the classifier or task router. On MTIL, accuracy improves from 84.7% to 85.9% with ViT-Base and from 71.1% to 74.5% with DEiT-Tiny; corresponding VDD improvements are 86.0% to 86.7% and 74.0% to 76.18%. ViT-Base inference FLOPs also decrease by approximately 9–10%.

Evaluation is substantial: two heterogeneous task streams, Base and Tiny backbones, three-seed main results, per-task breakdowns, additional CLIP experiments, task-order tests, and lightweight routing variants. These experiments support practical usefulness across different backbone capacities.

The sampling ablation provides evidence that HEE encourages parameter reuse. Table 9 reports substantially less parameter growth than uniform sampling while maintaining competitive accuracy. Architecture visualizations and tolerance-threshold experiments also substantiate the ability to trade accuracy for inference computation.

Overall, the raw accuracy and compute results provide a stronger case for acceptance than rejection, independently of the problematic FoM metric. The work offers a supported practical contribution, although several claims and reproducibility details require qualification.
weaknesses: The proposed FoM is unstable and should not support claims of being hundreds or thousands of times better. Its denominator is the accuracy gap to empirical full fine-tuning, which is neither a guaranteed upper bound nor noise-free. On VDD/Tiny, the denominator is only 0.03 percentage points, smaller than the reported variability. It becomes undefined at equality and can change sign when fine-tuning is surpassed, as CHEEM already does in the CLIP MTIL experiment. Moreover, it omits parameter storage, forgetting, and training cost despite being described as holistic.

The distinctive contribution of similarity-guided hierarchical sampling is only partly isolated. Uniform sampling already achieves comparable accuracy and slightly higher Tiny accuracy. Its greater parameter growth supports HEE's utility, but a task-independent reuse-biased sampler is missing, so the evidence does not distinguish useful task-similarity information from simply favoring reuse. There are also no individual New/Skip removal ablations or direct comparisons against the closely related L2G search approach.

Efficiency benefits involve meaningful costs. Table 7 reports 1.45 hours per task versus 0.38 for LoRA-CL and S-Prompts, approximately 3.8 times longer. Tiny inference FLOPs are essentially unchanged from LoRA-CL, while CLIP accuracy is below LoRA-CL on both benchmarks. These results support a conditional accuracy–compute trade-off rather than uniformly superior efficiency. Longer-stream storage and search scaling are not established.

The broad class-incremental framing exceeds the demonstrated setting: tasks are separate datasets with substantial distribution differences, making dataset identification especially useful. Table 19 shows that much of the gap to several prompting baselines comes from task/head selection. The matched LoRA comparison remains persuasive, but the results do not establish comparable advantages for strongly overlapping task distributions. The introduction's assertion that a shared classifier requires equal class counts is also incorrect.

Reproducibility has concrete gaps: the code URL is incomplete, and the manuscript does not specify the LoRA rank, routing centroid count, search population size, number of evolutionary iterations, or top-k setting. Tables 8 and 9 inconsistently report 0.40% versus 0.25% parameter growth for the same MLPDown configuration. Tables 17–18 list 19,850 CIFAR100 test images despite claiming official splits, which ordinarily contain 10,000. These discrepancies require clarification to reproduce the reported protocol.

strengths: CHEEM offers a useful integration of task-specific architecture search, parameter reuse, LoRA adaptation, and block skipping. Its explicit control of computation addresses a practical limitation of fixed-architecture continual learning.

The raw results support meaningful gains independently of the proposed metric. Against LoRA-CL, CHEEM improves MTIL accuracy from 84.7% to 85.9% with ViT-Base and from 71.1% to 74.5% with DEiT-Tiny; VDD gains are approximately 0.7 and 2.2 percentage points. ViT-Base inference FLOPs also decrease by approximately 9–10%.

Evaluation is reasonably substantial: two heterogeneous benchmarks, two backbone sizes, three-seed main results, additional CLIP experiments, task-order tests, and search hyperparameter studies. The lightweight routing experiments provide a useful deployment-oriented extension.

The uniform-sampling comparison supports a specific benefit of hierarchical sampling: substantially less parameter growth at broadly comparable accuracy. The learned architectures and tolerance sweep also demonstrate an interpretable accuracy–computation trade-off.
weaknesses: The headline Figure-of-Merit is mathematically fragile and does not justify claims of being many times better. Equation 6 divides by the gap to an empirical fine-tuning reference that is not a genuine upper bound. On DEiT-Tiny/VDD, the denominator is only 0.03 percentage points, below the reported variability, producing enormous ratios. The metric becomes undefined at equality and can change sign when the reference is exceeded—as already happens in the CLIP/MTIL results. It also omits training cost, parameter storage, and forgetting despite the holistic framing.

The incremental contribution over prior architecture-based continual learning is incompletely isolated. The paper acknowledges that L2G already searches reuse/adapt/new operations, but provides no direct comparison or closely matched implementation. There are no individual operation-removal ablations establishing the necessity of New or cross-task expert reuse. Table 9 supports parameter economy from HEE, but does not show consistent accuracy superiority: uniform sampling achieves 75.05% versus 74.51% on DEiT-Tiny.

Efficiency claims need narrower qualification. Table 7 reports 1.45 hours per task versus 0.38 for LoRA-CL and S-Prompts, approximately 3.8 times longer. DEiT-Tiny shows essentially no inference-FLOP reduction over LoRA-CL. Running every previous task network over the new training dataset to compute similarities also introduces a growing cost whose scaling is not evaluated. Total stored parameters and peak search memory are not compared comprehensively.

The evidence supports heterogeneous dataset-incremental learning more directly than general class-incremental learning. Table 19 shows that much of the dramatic advantage over several prompting baselines comes from task routing versus uncalibrated global classification. The matched-routing LoRA-CL baseline is therefore particularly informative, and its smaller gaps should anchor the claims. CLIP results further qualify universal superiority: CHEEM trails LoRA-CL in accuracy on both benchmarks while saving FLOPs.

Reproducibility has material gaps: the manuscript does not specify key settings such as LoRA rank, centroid count and precise routing rule, evolutionary population size, selection size, or search iterations. The code URL is incomplete. Dataset documentation lists 19,850 CIFAR100 test images despite claiming official splits, and Tables 8 and 9 disagree on ViT-Base parameter growth (0.40% versus 0.25%). These issues, together with incomplete attribution of the architectural contribution and the unreliable headline metric, place the paper at the decision boundary despite its credible empirical merits.

strengths: CHEEM provides a useful approach to exemplar-free continual visual recognition: task-conditioned architecture search combines reuse, LoRA adaptation, new modules, and skipping. Although these ingredients build on prior work, their integration with similarity-guided hierarchical sampling enables practical control over accuracy, parameter growth, and inference computation.

The strongest evidence is the comparison with LoRA-CL, which shares the adaptation location and task-centroid routing. On MTIL, CHEEM improves accuracy from 84.7% to 85.9% with ViT-Base and from 71.1% to 74.5% with DEiT-Tiny; on VDD, the corresponding improvements are 86.0% to 86.7% and 74.0% to 76.18%. ViT-Base inference FLOPs also decrease by approximately 9–10%. These comparisons support benefits beyond simply introducing task-specific heads.

Evaluation is substantial: two heterogeneous task streams, two backbone sizes, three-seed main results, additional CLIP experiments, per-task results, task-order experiments, and ablations of sampling, placement, and search tolerance. Table 9 supports the parameter-efficiency benefit of hierarchical sampling, particularly on DEiT-Tiny, where reported parameter growth falls from 14.93% to 6.32% with a modest accuracy trade-off.

The learned architectures and lightweight-router experiments demonstrate practical flexibility. Easier tasks receive more skipping, and using DEiT-Tiny for routing reduces ViT-Base MTIL FLOPs from 62.3 to 35.0 while retaining 84.2% accuracy. Overall, the direct accuracy–compute results support weak acceptance independently of the proposed FoM metric.
weaknesses: The FoM is mathematically fragile and does not justify the headline claims of being many times better. Equation 6 divides by the gap to independently fine-tuned performance, which is an empirical reference rather than a true upper bound. On VDD with DEiT-Tiny, this gap is only 0.03 percentage points, smaller than the reported variability, producing enormous ratios. The metric becomes undefined at equality and can change sign when the reference is exceeded, as occurs in the CLIP MTIL results. It also omits training cost, storage, and forgetting despite the holistic framing.

The specific contribution of task-synergy sampling is only partially isolated. HEE versus uniform sampling demonstrates reduced growth, but does not distinguish informative task similarities from a generic prior favoring reuse. There is also no direct comparison with the closely related Learn-to-Grow approach or systematic removal of individual operations. Table 9 actually favors uniform sampling in DEiT-Tiny accuracy, so HEE's demonstrated advantage is primarily parameter efficiency rather than uniformly better prediction.

The broad class-incremental claims exceed the demonstrated setting. Both benchmarks consist of identifiable dataset domains, which suit task-centroid routing; performance on class splits within a common domain is untested. Table 19 shows that much of the dramatic advantage over several prompting methods is associated with their global-head inference difficulty. The matched LoRA-CL comparison remains convincing, but the results do not establish similarly large gains across class-incremental settings. With CLIP, CHEEM also trails LoRA-CL in accuracy on both benchmarks while reducing FLOPs.

Efficiency has meaningful qualifications. Table 7 reports 1.45 hours per task versus 0.38 for LoRA-CL and S-Prompts, approximately 3.8 times the training cost. DEiT-Tiny has essentially unchanged inference FLOPs relative to LoRA-CL. Moreover, computing task similarities requires evaluating all previous task networks on each incoming dataset, leaving longer-stream scalability unresolved. Complete cumulative storage, including heads and centroid memory, is not reported alongside the main comparisons.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite useful optimizer and dataset descriptions. The manuscript omits concrete LoRA rank, centroid count and detailed routing settings, batch size, and evolutionary population size, iteration count, and selection count. The code link is only a GitHub placeholder. Reporting inconsistencies also need correction: Tables 8 and 9 give different ViT-Base parameter-growth values for the same apparent configuration, and Tables 17–18 list 19,850 CIFAR100 test images without explaining the departure from its standard 10,000-image test set. These are distinct from the conceptual limitations, but impede independent verification.
